title: Be still
hookLine: be still, and know that I am God (Psalm 46:10)
tomorrow: where does help come from, when you look up at the hills?
last: IN THEIR PLACE · AVOID, DO, PURIFY · CONTENTMENT IS WEALTH

cards: "Be still" shows up on mugs and pillows, next to a candle, as if it meant relax. But what does it mean when the whole world is shaking? The psalm it comes from has an answer.

Psalm 46 opens in an earthquake: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea."

teach.b: The psalm keeps shaking. Waters roar. Nations rage, kingdoms totter.

teach.h: BE STILL: LET GO, STOP FIGHTING.
teach.b: Then God breaks the bow, cuts the spear, burns the chariots, and speaks: "Be still, and know that I am God." Twice the psalm stops for a refrain: "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge."
The same company as the valley in Psalm 23. Who is told to be still? Many readers hear it said to the raging nations: stop.
Others hear it said to the people inside the shaking city too. Either way, it comes in the middle of the fight.
Some translators render the Hebrew verb as let go, or stop: drop your weapons, quit striving, and know who God is. Read that way, stillness is trust, not a calm mood.
Christians sing it that way in Martin Luther's hymn, A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, which he built on this psalm.

teach.h: STILL IN THE NOISE, NOT AFTER IT.
teach.b: A story told about Luther says that in hard times he'd turn to a friend and say: come, let's sing Psalm 46.
Not because the trouble stopped. Because it hadn't. Stillness in the middle of the noise, not after it.

how: Jews and Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of trouble; Lutheran and other Protestant churches sing Martin Luther's hymn A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, which is based on it.

o: sit perfectly motionless until your mind is blank
let go and stop striving, trusting God in trouble
wait quietly until every problem has passed

games.q: two weeks of lines: tap the pairs.
p: struck first; all tremble at the rod
a child knows it; an old man can't do it
lay on the skylight to hear Torah
built A Mighty Fortress on Psalm 46

s: in Psalm 46, be still means relax and think calm thoughts
it comes mid-fight, as the bow breaks: let go, stop striving, and know God.
Psalm 46 opens with the earth moving and mountains falling into the sea
though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea.
in Psalm 23, the dark valley never comes for those who trust
it walks through the valley; the promise is company: thou art with me.

games.q: the earth shakes, waters roar, nations rage. in Psalm 46, what comes right before 'be still'?
o: God breaks the bow, cuts the spear and burns the chariots.
the waters go calm and the sun comes out.
the people light candles and sit in silence.
games.why: God ends the fighting first; then be still. it's a word to stop striving, not a word to relax.

practice: Close your eyes and be still for the whole sit, and a minute after if you like. Don't try to make the noise stop: let sounds, thoughts and worries roar where they are. Just stop fighting them.
If you pray, you can say the line once: "Be still, and know that I am God."

wordCard.voice: Be still: Psalm 46's word in the middle of a fight. Let go, stop striving, and know who God is, while the waters still roar.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Psalm 46:11 in Hebrew numbering (46:10 in English): be still; some render it let go, or stop.

carryVoice: The line for this week's end: be still, even while it shakes. Two weeks of verses and psalms, gathered up.
